newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIA TO COMBAT CUSTOMS OFFICERS CORRUPTION.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIA TO COMBAT CUSTOMS OFFICERS CORRUPTION.

text.p: Bulgarian new customs chiefs said on Friday they had stepped up fight against corruption in their own ranks by tightening control and restructuring in line with the European Union's legal requirements.

"I have fired 50 officers for the last two weeks and it is an open secret that almost all customs chiefs will be replaced," the new head of the General Customs Directorate (GCD) Elka Vladova told a news conference.
She said some of them have already deposited their resignation.
Vladova said one of Bulgaria's main customs check-points, the port of Bourgas, was being audited and 249 cases of violations of the law had been already handed over to the prosecutors office.
"We want to be free from interference by influential institutions when we implement staff and structural changes," Vladova said.
She said by July 15 a draft customs law, in line with all legal requirements of the European Union, would be offered to the government for approval and then introduced for parliamentary approval.
The first step was taken on Friday after the Finance Ministry, which is the GCD's prinicpal, approved a new structure consisting of four customs regional directorates instead of 16, Vladova said.
"We will have one sea port customs directorate in the Black Sea port of Varna, one on the Danube River in the town of Rousse and two inside the country - in Sofia and Plovdiv," she added.
Last week police launched a lightning swoop on property owned by customs officers stationed at border check-points aimed at cracking down on ill-gotten gains.
The investigators checked whether the vehicles, real estate, land, huge houses and hard currency were lawfully owned.
The interior ministry said a large proportion of customs officers had "modern and new limousines and live in luxurious conditions.
Earlier on Friday Prime Minister Ivan Kostov appealed to parliament to amend laws in order to crack down on organised crime and corruption, which has run rampant since the collapse of communism.
Parliament is expected to begin debate shortly on tightening anti-crime laws.
Interior Minister Bogomil Bonev said recently that the Bulgarian legal system had only a limited ability to fight organised crime.

A National Human Development Report on Bulgaria, prepared by the United Nations' Development Programme, made available to Reuters, said "the link between corruption in the state administration and organised crime leads to the replacement of the state institutions by shadow power structures".
